239.title: Al-Quddus, the Most Holy
239.hook: the Most Holy, pure from every flaw
239.howItsDone: Muslims glorify Allah as al-Quddus in the prayer, some saying subbuhun quddus in the bowing or prostration, and subhan al-Malik al-Quddus three times after the witr prayer, following the Prophet's practice; ritual purity and a clean place are required for prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Malik, the King, and Umm Sulaym's question about a loan. Your line was everything is lent.

Musa is walking through the desert with his family, cold and lost. Far off, he sees a fire. Stay here, he tells them; maybe I can bring back a burning stick, or find someone who knows the way. He walks toward it. And when he gets close, the Qur'an says in Surah Ta Ha, he is called by name. O Musa. The voice tells him to do something first. Before the revelation, before the mission, before Pharaoh. One small, physical thing, because of where he's standing.
screen: `A FIRE IN THE DESERT.` → `O MUSA.` → `ONE THING FIRST.`

segments.voice: Take off your sandals, the voice says. You are in the holy valley, Tuwa. The word for holy there is muqaddas, from the root q-d-s, the same root as today's name. Al-Quddus: the Most Holy, the utterly pure, free from every flaw, every lack, everything unworthy. The name comes twice in the Qur'an, both times right beside yesterday's. At the end of al-Hashr, in Pickthall's words: the Sovereign Lord, the Holy One. And at the start of al-Jumu'ah, the same pair: al-Malik al-Quddus, the King, the Holy. The root runs through places Muslims love. Jerusalem is al-Quds, the holy, and an older name for it is Bayt al-Maqdis, the house of holiness. Musa told his people to enter al-ard al-muqaddasah, the holy land. And the Qur'an speaks of ruh al-qudus, the spirit of holiness, whom commentators identify with the angel Gabriel. What does holiness mean here? Scholars explain it as being set apart and pure: above anything the mind can imagine, and free of the flaws people find in themselves. So in the bowing of the prayer, Muslims may say words the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said there, which Muslim records: subbuhun quddus, glorified, holy, Lord of the angels and the Spirit. And after the night prayer of witr, he would say three times: subhan al-Malik al-Quddus. Glory to the King, the Holy. Notice what Musa is asked to do in the presence of the holy. Not a speech. He is asked to take something off. Holiness asks for a little clearing.
screen: `TAKE OFF YOUR SANDALS.` · `Q-D-S — HOLY, PURE, SET APART.` · `AL-QUDS, THE HOLY LAND, THE SPIRIT.` · `SUBBUHUN QUDDUS IN THE BOWING.` · then, large: `THE PURE ONE.`

segments.voice: Find one small space near you, a corner of a desk, a windowsill, a patch of floor, and clear it, wiping it if it needs it. Then sit near it in the quiet, no phone, no noise, shoes off if you like, as Musa was told, and notice how a cleared space changes the air around it. If you pray, you can say softly, subhan al-Malik al-Quddus.
Al-Quddus. The Most Holy, pure and set apart from every flaw; the root of al-Quds and of the holy valley where Musa was told to take off his sandals. Today's word.
Your line: the pure one. No flaw, no lack, nothing unworthy at all. See you tomorrow.

240.title: As-Salam, Peace itself
240.hook: Peace itself, the source of the greeting you've been saying since day one
240.howItsDone: Muslims greet one another with as-salamu 'alaykum and answer wa 'alaykum as-salam; every prayer ends with the greeting of peace and a turn of the head, and after it, following the Prophet's practice, people often say Allahumma anta s-Salam wa minka s-salam.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Quddus, and Musa's sandals in the holy valley. Your line was the pure one.

As-salamu 'alaykum. You learned it at the very start of this path. Peace be upon you. It turns up everywhere: at a mosque door, on a phone call, in a shop, shouted across a parking lot. And the answer, wa 'alaykum as-salam, and upon you, peace. It's said so often it can shrink to a blur, salamlekum, the way good morning becomes morning. But salam isn't only a wish. As-Salam is one of the most beautiful names, and a saying in al-Bukhari's al-Adab al-Mufrad calls it a name of Allah placed on the earth. So some hear His name passing between two people each time.
screen: `AS-SALAMU 'ALAYKUM.` → `SAID EVERYWHERE.` → `A NAME PASSING BETWEEN TWO PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: At the end of al-Hashr, right after the King and the Holy One, Pickthall's translation has a single word: Peace. As-Salam. Its root, s-l-m, means more than quiet: safe, sound, whole, unbroken. A salim heart is a sound one. Islam, submission, and Muslim come from the same root. So as-Salam is the one who is whole and free from every harm, and the source of every wholeness anyone else has. Some scholars say the greeting means both: the peace of Allah be on you, and Allah, who is Peace, be with you. Peace wraps the prayer too. Every prayer ends with as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah, said with a turn of the head: to the right and then the left, or in one school's practice to the right alone. Muslim records that after finishing, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ would say: O Allah, You are Peace, and from You is peace. Blessed are You, Owner of majesty and honor. The Garden has the same name: in Surah Yunus, Allah calls to dar as-salam, the home of peace. And the Prophet made the greeting a path to love. In Sahih Muslim he said: you will not enter the Garden until you believe, and you won't believe until you love one another. Shall I tell you something that, if you do it, will make you love one another? Spread salam among yourselves. Not a slogan. A practice, for people you know and people you don't.

segments.voice: Turn your head gently to the right, as the prayer's closing greeting does, think of someone close, and silently wish them peace, whole and unbroken. Then turn to the left and think of someone you find difficult, or someone you don't know at all, the cashier, the neighbor, and wish them peace too. Face forward and let the peace settle in the middle; if you pray, you can say, Allahumma anta s-Salam, O Allah, You are Peace.
As-Salam. Peace itself, the whole and the unharmed, the source of all peace, and the first word of the greeting. Today's word.
Your line: peace is his name. Salaam, peace or a real hello: the wish is the same. Day two hundred forty, done.

241.title: Al-Mu'min, the Giver of Safety
241.hook: the Giver of Safety and faith
241.howItsDone: Muslims describe the believer, the mu'min, by how safe others are around them, and treat promises, secrets and anything left in their care as an amanah, a trust; al-Amin, the trustworthy, was the Prophet's nickname in Mecca.

segments.voice: Yesterday, As-Salam, Peace itself, the name inside the greeting. Your line was peace is his name.

Who would you call at three in the morning? Not the funniest friend or the smartest one. The safe one: the one who wouldn't tell anyone, wouldn't make you feel stupid, would just pick up. Long before the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ received any revelation, the people of Mecca had a nickname for him. They left their valuables with him when they traveled. They called him al-Amin, the trustworthy one, the safe one. Today's name comes from the same three letters, and you already know it as the word for a believer.
screen: `THE ONE YOU'D CALL AT 3AM.` → `AL-AMIN, THE TRUSTWORTHY.` → `THE SAME THREE LETTERS.`

segments.voice: The root is a-m-n, and it grows a whole family. Amn: safety, the absence of fear. Amanah: a trust, something left in your keeping. Iman: faith. Amin: trustworthy. And the word Muslims say after the Fatiha, amin, so be it. At the end of al-Hashr, after Peace, comes al-Mu'min. Pickthall translates it the Keeper of Faith, and scholars give the name two meanings that sit together. First, the one who grants safety. The Qur'an says in Surah Quraysh that the Lord of the House fed them against hunger and made them safe from fear. Safety from fear is His gift. Second, the one who confirms: who affirms the truth of His messengers and keeps faith with His promises. He never breaks trust. Now the surprise. Mu'min is also the everyday word for a believer, a person of faith. The same word names Allah and names the people who trust Him. And the Prophet tied the two together in a very practical way. Tirmidhi and Nasa'i record him saying: the mu'min is the one from whom people's lives and property are safe. Another hadith, in Bukhari: the Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe. So a believer, in this sense, isn't first someone who holds the right ideas. It's someone people feel safe around. The name tells you what the one you trust is like, and what the one who trusts is meant to become.

segments.voice: Remember a time you felt completely safe with someone, where you were and what they did or didn't do, and let the feeling come back into your body: the shoulders dropping, the breath getting longer. Stay there for a few breaths. Then think of one person who might not feel safe right now, at home, at work, in their own head, and what would make them feel even a little safer around you: a kept secret, a calm voice, showing up when you said you would.
Al-Mu'min. The Giver of Safety, who grants safety from fear and keeps faith; also the word for a believer. Today's word.
Your line: the one who makes safe. A kept secret is a small amanah. Rest well.

242.title: Al-Khaliq, the Creator
242.hook: the Creator, who makes from nothing
242.howItsDone: Muslims affirm Allah as al-Khaliq, the Creator of everything from nothing, and reflect on creation as a sign; the name appears in names like Abdul-Khaliq, and the first revealed verses, read in the name of your Lord who created, are widely memorized.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Mu'min: the Giver of Safety, and the believer people feel safe around. Your line was the one who makes safe.

Before a tailor makes a single cut, the cloth lies on the table. The tailor measures, marks with chalk, measures again. Nothing is sewn yet, but in a way the coat already exists, in the measuring. Classical Arabic dictionaries record a word for exactly that moment: khalaqa, to measure out leather or cloth before cutting it. It became the Qur'an's word for creating. The verses tradition counts as the first revelation, the ones from camp four, use it twice in two lines: read, in the name of your Lord who created, created the human from a clinging clot. Today: Al-Khaliq, the Creator.
screen: `A TAILOR MEASURING CLOTH.` → `KHALAQA — TO MEASURE OUT.` → `READ, IN THE NAME OF YOUR LORD WHO CREATED.`

segments.voice: The name opens the last verse of al-Hashr. Here is Pickthall: He is Allah, the Creator, the Shaper out of naught, the Fashioner. Three names in a row, and scholars, al-Ghazali among them, read them as three movements. Al-Khaliq, today: the one who determines, measures and plans what will be. Al-Bari', the Shaper out of naught: the one who brings it into being. Al-Musawwir, tomorrow's name: the one who gives it its form. What makes the first more than a tailor? A tailor measures cloth that already exists. Muslim theologians teach that Allah creates from nothing at all: no cloth, no table, no chalk. When He wills a thing, the Qur'an says, He only says to it, be, kun, and it is. Kun fa-yakun. And the Qur'an doesn't place creation only at the beginning. It speaks of Allah creating again and again: every birth, every morning, every seed that splits. In this picture, a person didn't just happen once; they are held in being now. A curious detail: the Qur'an sometimes uses the same verb for people. The prophet 'Isa, Jesus, says he shapes a bird from clay, by Allah's permission. And after describing a child forming in the womb, it says, blessed is Allah, the best of creators. People make things too, measuring and shaping what's already there. But making from nothing, and holding it in being, Muslim teaching gives to Allah alone. In that view, everything in sight today was made.
screen: `KHALIQ, BARI', MUSAWWIR.` · `THE ONE WHO MEASURES AND PLANS.` · `KUN FA-YAKUN — BE, AND IT IS.` · `THE BEST OF CREATORS.` · then, large: `MADE.`

segments.voice: Take a sheet of paper, a napkin, a bit of string or a few leaves, and slowly make one small thing: fold a boat, tie a knot, arrange three stones. Notice how much measuring happens first, your eyes planning, your fingers testing, then look at what you made and at the hands that made it, shaped long before you ever used them. If you pray, you can say, ya Khaliq, softly.
Al-Khaliq. The Creator, who measures out and brings into being from nothing, and who keeps creating. Today's word.
Your line: made. A cup, an apple, your own hand: in this view, all of it made. Day two hundred forty-two, done.

243.title: Al-Musawwir, the Fashioner
243.hook: the Fashioner, who shapes every face differently (59:24)
243.howItsDone: Muslims reflect on the variety of human faces, colors and languages as signs of the Fashioner; mosque art, shaped by scholarly discussion of image-making, tends to use calligraphy, geometry and plant forms rather than figures.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Khaliq: the Creator who measures, plans and brings into being. Your line was made.

A train station at rush hour: faces, faces, faces. Two eyes, a nose, a mouth, every single time. The same few parts, and no two alike. Add everyone alive now and everyone who lived before, and each face is still its own. How many ways can two eyes and a mouth be arranged? Apparently, enough. Right after the Creator, the same verse in al-Hashr names the one who gives each thing its shape. Today: Al-Musawwir, the Fashioner.
screen: `A TRAIN STATION FULL OF FACES.` → `THE SAME FEW PARTS.` → `NO TWO ALIKE.`

segments.voice: Pickthall calls al-Musawwir the Fashioner. The root is s-w-r, with the heavy s, sad, and it gives surah: form, shape, image, a different word from the surah of the Qur'an. Tasawwur, imagining, forming a picture in the mind, comes from the same root. So al-Musawwir gives every created thing its particular form: this face, this leaf, this fingerprint. In Al 'Imran, He is the one who shapes you in the wombs however He wills. In at-Taghabun: He shaped you, and made your shapes good. In al-Infitar, from the juz' just read: He created you, then fashioned you, then proportioned you, and in whatever form He willed, He put you together. In ar-Rum, the differences in people's languages and colors are called among His signs. Not a problem to be fixed. A sign. Because the word for image is from this root, Muslim scholars have long discussed making pictures of living beings. Some, drawing on hadith, discouraged it; others permit some kinds, like photographs. Mosque walls in that tradition carry calligraphy, geometry and vines rather than faces. Then a hadith turns the whole name around. Muslim records the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ saying: Allah does not look at your forms, your suwar, or your wealth. He looks at your hearts and your deeds. The Fashioner made every face, and then chose not to judge by it. That leaves a question for anyone who looks at faces.
screen: `S-W-R — FORM, SHAPE, IMAGE.` · `SHAPED IN THE WOMB, SHAPES MADE GOOD.` · `COLORS AND LANGUAGES AS SIGNS.` · `HE LOOKS AT HEARTS, NOT FORMS.` · then, large: `EVERY FACE SHAPED.`

segments.voice: Hold up one hand and look closely: the lines across the palm, the creases at each knuckle, the whorls at your fingertips, a pattern nobody else has. Bring to mind a face you love and find one detail you've never really looked at, a laugh line, an eyebrow, the way the mouth rests. Give the same slow look to a face you passed today and barely saw, then to your own: one of a kind, never made before and never again.
Al-Musawwir. The Fashioner, who gives every created thing its own form, and every face its own shape. Today's word.
Your line: every face shaped. Even the ones passed without a look. See you tomorrow.

244.title: Al-Ghaffar, the Forgiving
244.hook: the Forgiving, again and again, however often you return
244.howItsDone: Muslims say astaghfirullah, I ask Allah's forgiveness, many times a day: after each prayer (often three times), at small slips, and in longer forms like sayyid al-istighfar, following the Prophet's practice of seeking forgiveness more than seventy times a day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Musawwir: the Fashioner who shaped every face, and who looks at hearts, not forms. Your line was every face shaped.

The same old thing. A temper that flares at the same person. A habit quit eleven times. A promise to oneself broken every Tuesday. The first time, asking forgiveness comes easily. By the fifth, it can feel embarrassing. By the twentieth, a person might stop asking at all, sure there's a limit and sure they've hit it. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told a story about exactly this person: a servant who does the same wrong again and again, and keeps coming back. Bukhari and Muslim both record it, and the answer is a name built for repetition. Today: Al-Ghaffar, the Forgiving.
screen: `THE SAME OLD THING.` → `THE TWENTIETH TIME.` → `SURELY THERE'S A LIMIT?`

segments.voice: In the story, a servant sins and says: my Lord, I have sinned, forgive me. And Allah says: My servant knew that he has a Lord who forgives sins and holds to account for them. I have forgiven My servant. Time passes. The servant does it again, with the same words, and gets the same answer: forgiven. A third time, the same. Scholars explain the story carefully: it isn't permission to do wrong. It's about the one who keeps sincerely turning back, meaning it each time. For that person, the door doesn't close. The root of the name is gh-f-r, to cover. A mighfar is a helmet, the thing that covers the head and protects it in battle. So forgiveness, maghfirah, is more than a pardon: the wrong is covered over, and you're protected from its harm. Three names of Allah come from this root. Al-Ghafir, the one who forgives. Al-Ghafur, whose forgiveness is great. And al-Ghaffar, built on a form that means again and again, as often as it's needed: the name for the twentieth time. The prophet Nuh told his people: ask your Lord for forgiveness; He is ever Ghaffar. And Bukhari records the Prophet saying that he himself asked Allah's forgiveness more than seventy times a day. If he did, the fifth time is no reason for embarrassment. Astaghfirullah: I ask Allah's forgiveness. Muslims say it after prayers, at small slips, and in the middle of ordinary days.

segments.voice: Let your same old thing come to mind and look at it honestly, the way you'd look at a scrape on your knee, without flinching or arguing for it, noticing any tiredness or shame. Then picture it covered, gently, like a helmet over a head or a blanket over someone sleeping, and breathe under that covering. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, once, slowly, and mean it, even if you've said it for this a hundred times before.
Al-Ghaffar. The Forgiving, again and again: the one who covers wrongs as often as a person sincerely returns. Today's word.
Your line: forgiven again. The twentieth time is what the name is for. That's day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: Ar-Razzaq, the Provider
245.hook: the Provider, of bread and of every other kind of provision
245.howItsDone: Muslims say bismillah before eating and alhamdulillah after, thanking Allah as the Provider; many speak of their income, family and health as rizq, and pair effort with tawakkul, trust, in the spirit of tie your camel and trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Al-Ghaffar: the servant who kept returning, and was forgiven again. Your line was forgiven again.

Early morning: birds leaving a tree. They have no jobs or savings accounts. They don't know where breakfast is. They just go. And in the evening they come back, and somehow they've eaten. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ pointed at exactly that. Umar reports it, and Tirmidhi records it: if you relied on Allah as He truly should be relied on, He would provide for you as He provides for the birds. They go out in the morning hungry, and come back in the evening full. Notice one small word: they go out. Today: Ar-Razzaq, the Provider.
screen: `BIRDS LEAVING A TREE AT DAWN.` → `OUT HUNGRY, BACK FULL.` → `THEY GO OUT.`

segments.voice: Ar-Razzaq comes from the root r-z-q; its noun, rizq, means provision, whatever sustains you. Here is Pickthall's translation from Surah adh-Dhariyat: Lo! Allah! He it is that giveth livelihood, the Lord of unbreakable might. Like ghaffar yesterday, the form razzaq is built for repetition: provision given again and again. In Surah Hud, there is no creature moving on the earth whose provision isn't upon Allah, and He knows where it rests and where it's kept. The ant, the whale, the baby, the old man. Rizq is wider than bread. Teachers list other kinds beside food: health, knowledge, friends, a family, work, time, a good night's sleep, and faith itself. Bread is one door into a whole house of provision. Back to the birds. They're provided for, and they still fly out every morning. Muslim scholars read trust in Allah as including effort. Tirmidhi records a man asking whether to tie his camel or trust: tie it, and trust. That camel gets a day of its own soon. The work is yours; the provision comes from somewhere outside your control. Many Muslims describe that as a weight lifted: not lazier, just less frantic. This week has been a string of names: the Holy, Peace, the Giver of Safety, the Creator, the Fashioner, the Forgiving, and now the Provider. In the Qur'an's picture, a person is made, shaped, kept safe, forgiven, and fed. Seven days, one picture.
screen: `R-Z-Q — PROVISION, WHAT SUSTAINS.` · `EVERY CREATURE, EVERY DAY.` · `BREAD, HEALTH, KNOWLEDGE, FRIENDS.` · `THE BIRDS STILL GO OUT.` · then, large: `PROVIDED FOR.`

segments.voice: Think about the last thing you ate and trace it back, one breath for each link: who cooked or packed it, who drove it to the store, who grew and harvested it, where the rain came from that made it grow. Then add one other kind of provision in your life right now, a friend, a skill, a quiet hour, and hold both. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for them.
Ar-Razzaq. The Provider, who gives provision again and again to every creature: bread, and every other kind of rizq. Today's word.
Your line: provided for. The birds still go out, and they still come back full. Until tomorrow.
